entries.title: Sequence: harden the kernel before any chain integration
entries.body: The README's 10-step path put Solana programs at step 3. We reordered: the authorization kernel decides what is ever allowed to move value, so it must be trustworthy before anything anchors to it. Live-chain evidence is worthless if the thing emitting commitments has holes.

entries.title: Reservation expiry was never enforced in the execution guard
entries.body: validateExecutionBinding read no expiresAt, so stale RESERVED/COMMITTED reservations returned ok:true. Confirmed against seed data res_run496. Fixed by requiring an explicit `now` and adding a RESERVATION_EXPIRED check.

entries.title: velocityLimit was declared but never evaluated
entries.body: The field existed on the Mandate type and was set on seed data, but evaluateProposal never read it. Now enforced over a caller-supplied window of recent spend.

entries.title: Negative amounts returned ALLOW at the policy layer
entries.body: Every amount guard was one-sided (>), so -100 passed policy and was only caught downstream in reserve(). Added INVALID_AMOUNT lower-bound guards in both the policy and execution layers, plus a NaN guard in reserve().

entries.title: Kernel functions take explicit time; they never call new Date()
entries.body: A hidden wall-clock read is what allowed the expiry bug to sit undetected. Time is now an injected parameter so the kernel stays pure and testable.

entries.title: An ALLOW decision is never itself permission to move value
entries.body: The exact instruction must still match the evaluated action digest, amount, asset, chain, expiry, nonce and reservation. This is the thesis of the product and the reason the execution guard exists as a separate gate from policy evaluation.

entries.title: Available vault capital reflects every encumbrance
entries.body: total = available + reserved + escrowed + encumbered + settling + frozen. reconcileVault must report zero difference or the log is not trustworthy.

entries.title: Economic kernel is not yet reachable from any API route or page
entries.body: evaluateProposal and validateExecutionBinding are never called in production paths. Only reconcileVault, netObligations and failureScenarios are wired. The authorization engine is effectively dead code until Phase 1 adds /reservations and /authorizations routes.

entries.title: Console UI is template-literal HTML, not components
entries.body: 15 pages totalling 89 lines, built from giant inline HTML strings (app/policies/page.tsx has a 2496-char single line). It demonstrates information architecture but is a mockup, not a product.

entries.title: Store is a static seed array; data.ts only re-exports it
entries.body: lib/store/data.ts is `export * from './seed'`. There is no persistence and no event log. Replacing this with Postgres plus an append-only event log is the first item of Phase 1.

entries.title: Should the shared context server live inside the app or beside it?
entries.body: Currently a standalone package with its own build. Integrating into Next.js would couple memory availability to the app's lifecycle, which is undesirable for a tool that must run even when the app is down.

entries.title: Agents announce intent in shared context before non-obvious work
entries.body: Record a decision entry BEFORE making the change, not a summary after. The reasoning is the only part a future reader cannot reconstruct from the diff. If you stop mid-task, leave a handoff entry stating what is done, what is next, and the risk.

entries.title: Search shared context before editing code you did not write
entries.body: Code that looks wrong is usually a decision you cannot see from the code itself. Run context_recall on the area first, and again whenever something surprises you. This is the cheapest way to avoid re-solving a settled problem.

entries.title: A wrong context entry is worse than a missing one
entries.body: Record only what you verified, never speculation. Every entry is read as fact by someone who was not there. If you were wrong, supersede it loudly and say what changed — never quietly contradict an entry you did not write.

entries.title: Actor ids are stable and prefixed by kind
entries.body: Use agent:<name>, human:<name> or service:<name> and reuse the same id across all sessions and machines. A fresh id per session makes context look like it came from a crowd of one-off strangers and breaks attribution.

entries.title: A stopped agent must leave a handoff or the work is lost
entries.body: An agent that stops mid-task without a handoff entry is the most expensive failure mode: worse than one that never started, because a human or another agent must re-derive all the reasoning. Done / next / risk, always.

entries.title: Disagreements are resolved by superseding, not by picking silently
entries.body: When context_digest reports a topic as contested, two people recorded the same decision differently. Write a new decision that supersedes both and states the tradeoff, so the reasoning survives. If it truly needs a human, record a question naming the exact choice.

entries.title: Phase 3c: one policy-evaluation seam, not scattered 'if encrypted' branches
entries.body:
PRD 11.11 requires that a down enclave FAIL CLOSED and that 'no component may silently downgrade a confidential policy into an unrestricted approval'. That rule is only enforceable if 'is this confidential?' is a property of the evaluation REQUEST rather than an if at each call site. So: one PolicyEvaluator interface, two implementations (PublicPolicyEvaluator, and Arcium behind the same interface), one flag on one type, one gate.

PRD 11.10 binds an enclave output to six fields: policy version, action digest, vault, mandate, decision expiry, execution guard. These are now a TS interface with all six REQUIRED, so adding one to the PRD forces adding it to the type and an implementation cannot omit one and compile.

THE FALLBACK, precisely. The PRD says 'fail closed UNLESS a separately defined public-policy fallback exists'. Those readings reconcile only if the fallback is (a) declared per-call, never a global default someone wires up and forgets; (b) marked evaluator:'public' on the result; (c) tagged ENCLAVE_FALLBACK_USED. An untagged fallback IS the silent downgrade the clause forbids, because evidence would claim a confidentiality that never happened.

ALSO ADDED: SignerAdapter (wallet signer abstraction, the other Phase 3 requirement). It exists because the same economic intent must execute on Solana, Base and Tempo (PRD 4.2) and each signs differently; a caller depending on Keypair directly would force a per-chain rewrite of the execution guard, which is the most dangerous code we have. mayExecute keeps two questions SEPARATE: is policy satisfied, and can this wallet sign. A local keypair answering yes to both must still be refused when policy says no.

MUTATION AUDIT 6/6 caught (implicit downgrade, hidden fallback marking, skipped expiry, public-error-as-outage, guard token not re-derived, DENY reaching the signer). This is the standard F25/F28 failed.

entries.title: Phase 4 started: Space exists, and the agreement machine finally has a write path
entries.body:
TWO FINDINGS FROM GROUNDING PHASE 4 IN THE ACTUAL CODE.

1. SPACE WAS MISSING ENTIRELY. The word appears 35x in Microcosm's source and 0x in Mitra's domain types, while PRD 50 explicitly asks for the 'Space concept'. Its absence was not cosmetic: without a container there is no SCOPED authority, so a mandate/rule/evaluator defined for one engagement is implicitly global and an agent admitted to one job is admitted to all. That is the opposite of 13.1's 'bounded' and it is the containment property the policy enclave rests on. Now a real type in lib/domain/types.ts.

2. THE AGREEMENT MACHINE HAD NO WRITE PATH. canTransition/transition existed and were called ONLY from tests - no production code touched them. That is exactly Phase 0's recorded blocker, 'six of seven state machines lack write paths'. A transition table nothing consults is documentation with a type signature. lib/kernel/commerce.ts now routes every status change through transition(), which THROWS on an illegal edge so a caller that forgets to check cannot write the state anyway.

CONTainment DESIGN POINT: I added spaceId to the Agreement type. Without it containment was ADVISORY - applyAgreementOp(space, agreement, ...) takes the Space as an argument, so a caller can hand in the wrong one and every rule silently validates against a Space the agreement was never in. Storing the link makes a wrong Space DETECTABLE rather than a mistake people must remember to avoid. That is the difference between a check and a convention.

Refund is deliberately EXEMPT from the budget admission check: requiring headroom to give money back would strand it.

entries.title: EVM standards layer built: EIP-712, ERC-1271, ERC-8183, ERC-8004, x402/MPP, ERC-4337
entries.body:
Every ERC/EIP reference in this codebase used to be a counterparty string in seed.ts - x402:approved:*, erc8183:provider-3. That is the F24 pattern: seed data describing systems that did not exist. Now built.

EIP-712 is the load-bearing one. The Base settlement commitment was FNV-1a, honestly labelled NOT signature-grade - and that label is why the adapter was provisional, because a digest no signer can produce and no verifier can check is not a commitment. It is now a real typed-data digest over a domain separator (verified 32-byte keccak), so a settlement is a value a wallet can SIGN.

THE BUG THAT MATTERED, found by a test using a stub verifier: EOA signature recovery THROWS on a contract-wallet signature, and I was returning MALFORMED_SIGNATURE immediately - which made the entire ERC-1271 path unreachable and denied every smart-account signature. Exactly the silent denial the function exists to prevent. Fall-through is now the design.

ERC-8183 is a PROJECTION from Agreement/Deliverable/Reservation, not a second commerce system. One lifecycle, two vocabularies. It refuses an unbacked escrow, because an ERC-8183 consumer reads escrow as held funds.

ERC-8004 is projected OUTWARD only. Mitra never accepts a registry verdict on identity - a third party that could mint an agent into existence would bypass onboarding. Reputation is an ATTRIBUTED CLAIM that may influence only discovery RANKING. If a registry score could raise a spending limit, an attacker would buy a high score and spend against it, which is the unaudited credit system PRD 3.2 explicitly refuses.

x402/MPP: neither may move capital. Both issue instructions; the vault decides. A session REFUSES a charge past its ceiling, and every x402 challenge requires a reservation. Tempo receipt mapping refuses while token decimals are UNRESOLVED - converting without a scale is off by a power of ten, and a receipt wrong by 10^6 is worse than one never produced.

ERC-4337 is envelope only and the module header says so: packing, hashing, validation, batching by sender. No bundler, EntryPoint or paymaster is deployed and nothing has touched Base.

Mutations 8/8. TS 343 pass, Rust 72/72, tsc clean.
STILL NOT BUILT: the Virtuals marketplace adapter - the one Phase 5 item left.

entries.title: F40 — the F39 TIP-20 registry was itself fabricated (4 of 5 entries wrong)
entries.body:
Moderato has no USDC *and* no OUSD. Reading name() from a node gives PathUSD/AlphaUSD/BetaUSD/ThetaUSD at indices 0-3, plus OpenUSD at 0x20c0...6a37da5c996874be. F39 asserted OUSD@0, pathUSD@1, AlphaUSD@2, BetaUSD@6a37, ThetaUSD@3 — four of five wrong.

Why nothing caught it: the pinning test asserted expect(TEMPO_TOKENS).toEqual({...the same literals it replaced...}). Asserting a literal against the object it was copied from cannot fail for any reason other than someone editing the test. Two self-referential copies do not corroborate each other.

The literal assertion is DELETED, not rewritten. Replaced by property assertions (symbol equals key; no native symbol; exactly the verified set) plus an opt-in TEMPO_LIVE=1 test that re-derives every name() from rpc.moderato.tempo.xyz. Verified: 842ms of real network round-trips, 28/28 in file.

RULES ADDED: (4) a constant pinned by a literal is pinned to nothing; (5) correcting a fabrication is itself an unverified claim.

entries.title: F41 — a frozen vault could be drained
entries.body:
withdraw() did its arithmetic INLINE in the handler and, unlike its sibling reserve(), never checked is_frozen(). An emergency freeze did not stop the one operation it most needed to.

Why it survived: FR-VAULT-006 was recorded UNTESTED with the rationale "the invariant holds by absence: there is no withdrawal route at all". That was FALSE — withdraw had been in lib.rs the whole time. The missing thing was a test, not a path. An invariant discharged by a claimed absence nobody checked is a claim, not weaker evidence; it concealed the work.

Fix: rules moved into Vault::withdraw alongside deposit/reserve/release. The freeze asymmetry with release is deliberate and documented — release moves capital WITHIN the vault and must stay permitted or a freeze strands in-flight obligations; withdraw moves capital OUT, which is what a freeze exists to stop.

THE PART WORTH KEEPING: type tests alone did not catch it. A mutation restoring the pre-F41 handler shape left the ENTIRE Rust suite green (9 new tests, all 72 pre-existing). Two further tests now drive the real mitra_vault::dispatch with real AccountInfos and kill that mutation (2 failures). The negative case (an unfrozen vault MUST allow withdrawal) is included so always-refuse cannot pass either way.

RULES ADDED: (8) holds-by-absence must be checked, not assumed; (9) inline arithmetic in a handler bypasses every state-level guard.

entries.title: F42 — a Space budget was a lifetime cap; the fix allowed a double-release
entries.body:
committed was incremented on fund and NEVER decremented — not on acceptance, not on refund. Headroom is budget - committed, so a Space with a 100 budget could fund exactly ten 10-USDC agreements ACROSS ALL TIME; the eleventh failed with SPACE_BUDGET_EXCEEDED even though all ten had been accepted and paid for. Reproduction fails on agreement index 9.

Why nothing caught it: every commerce test drove ONE agreement to completion and asserted the resulting status. None asked what the Space could do NEXT.

THE SECOND DEFECT WAS INTRODUCED BY THE FIRST. ACCEPTED -> REFUNDED is a LEGAL edge in the machine table, and both are settlement states, so releasing on either without a flag returns the price TWICE. With other agreements still encumbered this manufactures headroom ABOVE the budget. escrowReleased on Agreement exists for exactly this.

The double-release nearly shipped untested: a mutation removing the if(agreement.escrowReleased) guard left 27 of 27 tests green. Only a test that places a chargeback next to two live agreements kills it.

Three fixture bugs in my own tests, each looking like a kernel defect: driveToAccepted returned only the agreement (stale Space), apply discarded r.value.space, and one assertion used the pre-fund Space. entries.title: F43 — the mandate circuit ALLOWED zero-amount actions and one reason for every DENY
entries.body:
Neither defect is visible in the artifact: the circuit compiles, its Rust unit test passes, and arcium build reports success. Both bugs live in the reason and validity arithmetic, which no test exercised.

DEFECT 1 — zero-amount actions were ALLOWED. is_nonzero(x) was not_gt(0, x), commented "which is exactly x >= 1". It is not: not_gt(0,x) is !(0 > x) which is x >= 0 — ALWAYS TRUE. So is_nonzero(0) returned 1, amount_ok was 1, and the guard four lines above ("a zero amount is never valid") never fired. x != 0 is x > 0.

DEFECT 2 — every DENY returned REASON_AMOUNT_INVALID. when_allowed(a,r,f) = a*r + (1-a)*f; when the decision fails a=0, so (1-a)=1 and the result is the fallback UNCONDITIONALLY. Reasons 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 were unreachable — the entire attribution mechanism the doc comment calls the point of the circuit.

DEFECT 2b — precedence inverted: when(is_zero(x), CODE, reason) ran unconditionally, so a LATER failure overwrote an earlier one. A dead mandate that also breached max_transaction blamed the limit.

Verified by extracting the arithmetic and simulating it (when(c,t,o)=c*t+(1-c)*o) rather than reasoning about it. Before: zero amount allowed=1; all four DENY cases reason=AMT. After: all 9 cases correct including the boundary amount==max_transaction and multi-failure precedence.

RULES ADDED: (12) a comment asserting an equivalence is a claim, not a proof — verify boundary values 0 and the limit, not the middle; (13) a constant can masquerade as a mechanism.

entries.title: F45 — the clearing commitment was FNV-1a over an AMBIGUOUS join
entries.body:
Phase 7 was blocked as PARTIAL because the clearing digest "is FNV-1a, not signature-grade". True, and the LESSER problem. The code was: const s = fields.join("|"); then FNV-1a over s.

STRUCTURAL AMBIGUITY: joining with "|" cannot distinguish a field that CONTAINS "|" from a field boundary. Verified: ["epoch_1","alice|bob","100"] and ["epoch_1","alice","bob|100"] both hash to fnv1a_eee9e662. Two different obligation sets produced the SAME commitment. This collision occurs BEFORE the hash width is considered, so swapping FNV-1a for SHA-256 while keeping join("|") would NOT have fixed it — a party could still submit two sets that agree. Fixing only the hash would have produced a signature-grade digest that is still trivially forgeable.

Fix: digest(domain, fields) delegates to typedHash — domain-separated SHA-256, already used for action digests and the §17.3 receipt chain. Passing the ARRAY lets canonicalize carry the structure, so boundaries are encoded rather than guessed. The domain became a REQUIRED parameter, so inputsRoot and resultHash cannot collide with each other.

Tests assert PROPERTIES not the output literal — pinning a string would repeat F40. Determinism and order-independence are asserted too, since a careless fix could have lost properties the old digest had. Mutation check: restoring the exact pre-F45 implementation fails 5 of them.

BREAKING: all clearing digest values change; previously recorded inputsRoot/resultHash are stale.

Phase 7 stays PARTIAL, now on EVIDENCE not code: no epoch has been finalized on a live network.

RULES ADDED: (15) a delimiter is a structural assumption, widening the hash does not help; (16) when a blocker names one weakness, test for the others.

F50a — armSaga, startSaga, recordStep and beginCompensation are all declared Result<Saga> and NONE is wrapped in a try; they call transition, which throws. PRD §4.5 is "failure is a state transition, not an exception" and these four ARE the recovery path — a caller trusting the signature gets an unhandled throw precisely when a saga is already in trouble. They were also INCONSISTENT: startSaga and recordStep returned fail() for their own checks but still let transition throw, so only SOME illegal calls produced a Result and a caller could not tell which. Fixed: all four are throwing primitives, asResult wrappers exported under the real names. transition still throws deliberately — it is the primitive. Found by a test asserting re-entering compensation is refused: the refusal was THROWN, so the test errored instead of observing a Result.

F50b — lib/kernel/commerce-recovery.ts. Commercial transition FIRST, saga second; a refused startExecution must not leave a saga EXECUTING. fund declares+arms a saga with a pre-committed REFUND route (§15.5); startExecution ARMED->EXECUTING; rejectDeliverable walks EXECUTING->STEP_FAILURE->COMPENSATING->RECOVERED and releases space.committed.

CAPITAL ORDERING: the refund releases committed capital BEFORE the saga goes terminal. Saga-fails-first means capital moves with no recorded reason; release-fails-first means the saga claims a recovery that never happened. Releasing first makes the worst case a saga that UNDER-reports recovery (visible) rather than capital that moved with no record (not).

DELIBERATE DISAGREEMENT with the handoff: it said declare a saga only if failurePolicy is present. We arm either way, defaulting an empty policy to "refund on expiry". §15.5 requires a saga with >1 step to declare a compensation route, and funding a two-step agreement is exactly that — so gating the recovery path on an optional prose field would let a blank field leave escrow with no unwind.

entries.title: mitra-vault: any signer can issue a permit against any mandate, and a permit can spend a vault its holder does not own
entries.body:
VERIFIED in-process against the real mitra_vault::dispatch, with real AccountInfos, rustc 1.98.1. NOT exercised on devnet.

GAP 1, spend_authorized (lib.rs ~771): there is no check that vault_account belongs to the permit's holder. It checks program ownership of vault, authorization and mandate, and checks authorization.holder == mandate.holder. It never checks vault.authority == mandate.holder, and never re-derives the vault PDA from the holder. Repro: the attacker opens their own mandate and permit, then passes the victim's vault PDA. The result is Ok(()), the attacker receives 5000 lamports, and the victim's available drops 10000 to 5000. The existing tests/spend_integration.rs fixture already builds the vault with Vault::new(Pubkey::new_unique(), ...), an authority unrelated to the holder, so the suite has been passing over this.

GAP 2, authorize (lib.rs ~631): policy_engine only has to be a signer. The program never checks that it is the holder, or any key recorded on the mandate. Repro: a stranger key issues a 5000-unit permit against the victim's mandate, and the result is Ok(()). This contradicts ADR-0009 decision 2 ('Only the program may author an Authorization. The kernel may propose') and the open_mandate doc comment ('it cannot mint a permit').

COMBINED: the recipient is a caller-chosen account that neither the permit nor action_hash binds. With gap 2 alone, anyone can issue permits against a victim's mandate with fresh action_hashes and spend the victim's vault to themselves, one mandate.limit at a time. Fixing gap 1 alone does NOT close this.

IMPACT ON MY WORK: I am not binding SolanaSettlementAdapter to spend_authorized until this is fixed. A settlement transport over a drainable vault would put a live claim on top of it.

WHO: the deployed program GkQQtmVX... has upgrade authority C4ZoTdNSPkC6WeAPZQ4kXVDyvrZ5NY7YCxvMUY2pSefD (the lead). Only the lead can redeploy. Repro tests are in my scratchpad, ready to become regression tests on a fix branch.

FIX SHAPE, not applied, for discussion: (a) spend_authorized re-derives the vault PDA from mandate.holder and checks vault.authority; (b) authorize requires the holder to sign, or a policy-engine key recorded on the mandate at open time; (c) bind the recipient into the permit (store it, or require action_hash to commit to it) so a valid permit cannot be redirected.

entries.title: Fixing mitra-vault permit binding on fix/vault-permit-binding — code and tests only, NOT deployed
entries.body:
Fix for blocker ctx_378e7a61eb6fbf6b. Branch fix/vault-permit-binding, cut from fix/integrity-f40-f45 at 0691338. No deploy: only the lead (C4ZoTdNS...) can upgrade GkQQtmVX....

A THIRD GAP found while designing the fix: spend_authorized requires no signer at all, and the recipient is caller-chosen. So any observer can redeem any unspent on-chain permit to themselves.

DESIGN, following the PRD ('the principal's mandate'; authority.create({agentId,...}) is the principal's call; an agent spend vault is 'linked to one agent mandate') and ADR-0009 decision 2:
- Mandate gains principal + policy_engine. open_mandate is signed by the PRINCIPAL, who must be the authority of the named vault. The agent no longer grants itself a mandate. This reverses the 'self-binding by holder' comment, deliberately.
- authorize: the signer must equal mandate.policy_engine. Takes a recipient, which is stored in the Authorization.
- spend_authorized: the vault must be the PDA of mandate.principal, with matching authority, and the recipient must equal authorization.recipient.
- amend_mandate: the principal may amend or revoke. The holder may ONLY revoke (it can stop itself but not widen itself).

Decisions and answers to Purple's Seq 53 & Seq 54 questions:

1. EVM VAULT SIGNING KEYS:
For testnet execution (Base Sepolia & Tempo Moderato), use the local relayer execution key (.dev-keys/evm-testnet.key) operating as an authorized relayer under the mandate's pre-committed spend limits. - (1) Principal as signer on open_mandate: APPROVED. Reversing 'self-binding by holder' is correct and normative per PRD §3.
- (2) Holder may only revoke itself: APPROVED. An agent may stop itself, but never widen its limits.

entries.body:
Sprint item 1 is done on feat/settlement-caller (uncommitted at time of writing). Nothing is merged.

HOW IT WORKS
- The caller supplies agreementId + reservationId. Amount, asset, chain, payee and digest are all re-derived from the agreement.
- lib/kernel/settlement.ts runs, in order: assertSettlementBinding (ACCEPTED, not already settled); payTo present; reservation.agreementId matches; the mandate is the client's, on this vault, ACTIVE and unexpired; the vault is not frozen; the vault's chain is the payTo chain. Then it re-runs validateExecutionBinding against agreementPaymentDigest (capability fixed to "payment"; agreementId bound into actionDigestFor, and omitted when absent so existing digests are unchanged).
- lib/settlement/settle-agreement.ts then: checks the rail exists and vault.address === rail.payer; claims the settlement (id = set_<agreementId>, insert-only, so the primary key gives at most one per agreement); consumes the nonce; broadcasts; verifies; sets agreement.settledRef.
- A transport error leaves the settlement PENDING (outcome unknown) and blocks retries. FAILED is written only when nothing can have been sent. An unconfirmed transfer returns 202 SUBMITTED, and op=confirm re-checks it.
- Rails come from the environment only (lib/settlement/rails.ts). An unconfigured rail returns 503 before anything is claimed. There is no fallback transport.

entries.body:
NEEDS LEAD. No route in app/api authenticates its caller. There is no middleware, no header check and no actor binding. So /api/v1/agreements applies acceptDeliverable for anyone, including the agreement's own provider. Since sprint item 1, POST /api/v1/settlements pays an ACCEPTED agreement. A provider that can reach the API can therefore approve its own payout.

CURRENT CONTAINMENT (this is not authorization): settlement pays only the agreement's payTo term, from a reservation that policy approved for that provider and price. The x402 gateway pays only the payee bound into a reservation's digest. A caller can trigger these payments but cannot redirect them.

DECISION (human:purple, 2026-10-04): the live MCP server withholds mitra_fund_agreement, mitra_accept_deliverable and mitra_reject_deliverable until the API identifies callers.

PROPOSED FIX, which is the lead's call:
- A caller identity on the API: per-agent credentials, or signed requests. verifyAuthorisation plus RpcSignatureVerifier now verify EOA, ERC-1271 and ERC-6492 signatures on chain.
